Timothy S. Robbins et al › Filing 6 Jelber Ediveth Diaz Osorio v. Timothy S. Robbins et al, No. 2:2026cv00757 - Document 6 (C.D. Cal. 2026) Full Name: Jelber Ediveth Diaz Osorio v. Timothy S. Robbins et al Docket Number: 2:2026cv00757 Date: January 27, 2026 Court Description: ORDER GRANTING EX PARTE APPLICATION FOR TEMPORARY RESTRAINING ORDER ANDORDER TO SHOW CAUSE 2 by Judge Otis D. Wright, II: For the reasons discussed above, the Court GRANTS Petitioners TRO. (Dkt. No. 2.) It is hereby ORDERED that: Respondents shall IMMEDIATELY RELEASE Petitioner; Respondents are ENJOINED from re-detaining Petitioner absent compliance with constitutional protections, which include, at a minimum, pre-deprivation notice and a hearing before a neutral arbiter. At any such hearing, Respondents shall bear the burden of establishing that Petitioner poses a risk of flight or danger to the community; and Respondents shall SHOW CAUSE, in writing only, to be received by the Court no later than February 3, 2026, as to why the Court should notissue a preliminary injunction in this case. Petitioner may file a reply byFebruary 6, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. The Court SETS a hearing on the preliminary injunction for February 10, 2026, at 10:00 a.m., via Zoom. (lc) Download PDF Jelber Ediveth Diaz Osorio v. Timothy S. Robbins et al Case 2:26-cv-00757-ODW-AGR Doc. 6 Document 6 #:90 Filed 01/27/26 Page 1 of 9 Page ID O 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 United States District Court Central District of California 9 10 11 JELBER EDIVETH DIAZ OSORIO, 12 13 14 15 Petitioner, v. TIMOTHY S. ROBBINS et al., Case 26-cv-00757-ODW (AGRx) ORDER GRANTING EX PARTE APPLICATION FOR TEMPORARY RESTRAINING ORDER AND ORDER TO SHOW CAUSE [2] Respondents. 16 17 I. INTRODUCTION 18 Petitioner Jelber Ediveth Diaz Osorio brings a petition for a writ of habeas 19 corpus against Respondents Timothy S. Robbins, Director of Los Angeles Field Office 20 of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (“ICE”); Todd Lyons, Acting Director of 21 ICE; U.S. Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”); Kristi Noem, Secretary of the 22 DHS; David Marin, Warden of Adelanto ICE Processing Center; and Pamela Bondi, 23 U.S. Attorney General. (Pet. ¶¶ 12–18, Dkt. No. 1.) Petitioner also moves ex parte 24 for a temporary restraining order requiring his immediate release from custody. (Ex 25 Parte Appl. (“TRO”) 15, Dkt. No. 2.) Respondents fail to timely oppose the request. 26 For the reasons discussed below, the Court GRANTS the TRO. 27 28 Dockets.Justia.com Case 2:26-cv-00757-ODW-AGR 1 Document 6 #:91 II. Filed 01/27/26 Page 2 of 9 Page ID BACKGROUND 2 Petitioner is a citizen of Colombia. (Pet. ¶ 20.) On March 23, 2023, he arrived 3 in the United States to seek asylum along with his now spouse, Luisa Fernanda Paz 4 Cuellar, and their infant child. (Id. ¶ 22.) That same day, Respondents arrested 5 Petitioner and his family. (Id.) On March 26, 2023, Respondents released them. (Id.) 6 Respondents required Petitioner to enroll in the Intensive Supervision Appearance 7 Program (“ISAP”) and check-in with ICE. (Id. ¶ 24.) Respondents later placed 8 Petitioner in removal proceedings pursuant to 8 U.S.C. § 1229a. (Id. ¶ 23.) 9 On April 13, 2023, Petitioner appeared at ICE’s office as instructed. (Id. ¶ 25.) 10 ICE then scheduled Petitioner for monthly in-person visits at the ISAP office and 11 instructed him to take a picture of himself and send it to ICE weekly via a monitoring 12 application. (Id.) Petitioner complied with Respondents’ instructions. (Id. ¶ 26.) 13 On June 16, 2023, Petitioner and his family relocated to Santa Clara, California. 14 (Id. ¶ 27.) ICE then instructed Petitioner to attend monthly check-ins at the ISAP 15 office and continue to send pictures of himself to ICE. (Id.) Petitioner continued to 16 comply with all his monitoring requirements. (Id. ¶ 28.) 17 In April 2024, Petitioner and his family relocated again. (Id. ¶ 28.) ICE then 18 instructed Petitioner to present himself in person at the ISAP office in Camarillo, 19 California. (Id.) When Petitioner appeared at the ISAP office, ICE placed a wrist 20 monitor on him. (Id.) ICE instructed Petitioner to start taking and sending pictures of 21 himself with the wrist monitor on a weekly basis. (Id.) ICE scheduled Petitioner for 22 monthly in-person visits at the ISAP Camarillo office. (Id.) 23 On March 17, 2025, ICE removed Petitioner’s wrist monitor and instructed him 24 to continue sending pictures of himself via the monitoring application. (Id. ¶ 29.) 25 ICE told Petitioner they would contact him by phone every fifteen days, and Petitioner 26 was required to be at home when the call occurred. (Id.) ICE also required Petitioner 27 to attend in-person check-ins at the ISAP field office every fifteen days. (Id.) 28 2 Case 2:26-cv-00757-ODW-AGR 1 Document 6 #:92 Filed 01/27/26 Page 3 of 9 Page ID Petitioner complied with all requirements of his release. (Id.) However, 2 starting in April 2025, Petitioner began experiencing issues with the monitoring 3 application. (Id. ¶ 30.) On a few occasions when Petitioner tried to send his pictures, 4 he received an error stating that his face was not detected. (Id.) Whenever this 5 happened, Petitioner contacted his assigned ICE officer by phone and informed her of 6 the problem. (Id.) Petitioner also went in person to the ISAP office to complain about 7 the application issues. (Id.) Petitioner’s assigned ICE officer always acknowledged 8 that the application might have technical problems and told Petitioner that he was still 9 in compliance with the monitoring program. (Id.) 10 Petitioner also continued to actively work on his immigration case. (Id. ¶ 31.) 11 Specifically, Petitioner filed an asylum application with the San Francisco 12 immigration court. (Id.) He later applied for and obtained employment authorization 13 and social security card. (Id.) Petitioner and his spouse began working as full-time 14 delivery drivers, which permitted them to cover the household expenses and save 15 money for an immigration attorney. (Id. ¶ 32.) 16 On December 23, 2025, Petitioner appeared for his scheduled check-in at the 17 ISAP office. (Id. ¶ 33.) At the end of that visit, Petitioner was instructed to appear at 18 the ICE office in Camarillo. (Id.) Petitioner complied and appeared at the ICE office 19 to what he believed to be a routine check-in. (Id.) However, upon his arrival, ICE 20 detained Petitioner. (Id.) Prior to Petitioner’s re-detention, ICE did not provide him 21 with notice of the revocation of his parole. (Id. ¶ 34.) As of the date of this Order, 22 Petitioner has not received a hearing before a neutral decisionmaker to determine if 23 his re-detention is justified. (Id. ¶ 35.) 24 Based on these allegations, on January 24, 2026, Petitioner filed a Petition for 25 Writ of Habeas Corpus on the grounds that his re-detention violates his Fifth 26 Amendment right to due process. (Id. ¶¶ 48–51.) That same day, Petitioner filed this 27 Application for a Temporary Restraining Order. (TRO.) Petitioner requests that the 28 Court order Respondents to immediately release Petitioner from custody. (Id. at 15.) 3 Case 2:26-cv-00757-ODW-AGR Document 6 #:93 III. 1 Filed 01/27/26 Page 4 of 9 Page ID LEGAL STANDARD 2 A temporary restraining order (“TRO”) is an “extraordinary remedy that may 3 only be awarded upon a clear showing that the plaintiff is entitled to such relief.” 4 Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, 555 U.S. 7, 22 (2008). The standard for issuing a 5 TRO is “substantially identical” to that for a preliminary injunction. Stuhlbarg Int’l 6 Sales Co. v. John D. Brush & Co., 240 F.3d 832, 839 n.7 (9th Cir. 2001). Pursuant to 7 Federal Rule of Civil Procedure (“Rule”) 65, a court may grant preliminary injunctive 8 relief to prevent “immediate and irreparable injury.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 65(b). To obtain 9 relief, a plaintiff must meet the “Winter” factors: (1) the plaintiff “is likely to succeed 10 on the merits”; (2) the plaintiff “is likely to suffer irreparable harm in the absence of 11 preliminary relief”; (3) “the balance of equities tips in [the plaintiff’s] favor”; and 12 (4) “an injunction is in the public interest.” Am. Trucking Ass’ns, Inc. v. City of Los 13 Angeles, 559 F.3d 1046, 1052 (9th Cir. 2009) (quoting Winter, 555 U.S. at 20). IV. 14 DISCUSSION The Court briefly addresses its jurisdiction to review Petitioner’s claims, before 15 16 turning to the merits of the TRO. 17 A. Jurisdiction 18 The Court must first consider whether it has jurisdiction to review Petitioner’s 19 TRO. See Sinochem Int’l Co. v. Malaysia Int’l Shipping Corp., 549 U.S. 422, 430–31 20 (2007) (“[A] federal court generally may not rule on the merits of a case without first 21 determining that it has jurisdiction.”). Under 8 U.S.C. § 1252(g), a court does not 22 have jurisdiction to review “any cause or claim” challenging the execution of 23 “removal orders.” However, a “district court may consider a purely legal question that 24 does not challenge” the execution of a removal order. United States v. Hovsepian, 25 359 F.3d 1144, 1155 (9th Cir. 2004). 26 Here, Petitioner raises a question of law as to whether his re-detention complies 27 with due process and there is no underlying final removal order in this case. (See 28 generally TRO.) As such, the Court does not review the Attorney General’s authority 4 Case 2:26-cv-00757-ODW-AGR Document 6 #:94 Filed 01/27/26 Page 5 of 9 Page ID 1 to execute removal proceedings. Instead, the Court confines its analysis to the narrow 2 legal question properly before it: whether Petitioner’s re-detention violates his right to 3 due process. As the Court addresses only the legality of Petitioner’s re-detention, the 4 Court has jurisdiction to review Petitioner’s TRO. See Hovsepian, 359 F.3d at 1155. 5 Moreover, under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, the Court has authority to adjudicate a 6 habeas corpus petition alleging that a person is being held in custody “in violation of 7 the Constitution or laws or treaties of the United States.” “[T]he essence of habeas 8 corpus is an attack by a person in custody upon the legality of that custody, and that 9 the traditional function of the writ is to secure release from illegal custody.” Preiser v. 10 Rodriguez, 411 U.S. 475, 484 (1973). Here, Petitioner alleges that his re-detention 11 without notice and a pre-deprivation hearing before a neutral decisionmaker violates 12 his constitutional right to due process. (Pet. ¶¶ 48–51.) Thus, Petitioner also properly 13 invokes the Court’s habeas jurisdiction. 14 B. 15 16 Merits of the TRO: Winter Factors Having determined that the Court has jurisdiction over Petitioner’s TRO, the Court now turns to its merits under the Winter factors. 17 1. Likelihood of Success on the Merits 18 The first Winter factor “is the most important,” and “is especially important 19 when a plaintiff alleges a constitutional violation and injury.” Baird v. Bonta, 81 F.4th 20 1036, 1040 (9th Cir. 2023). Petitioner argues that he is likely to succeed on the merits 21 because his detention violates his due process rights. (TRO 7.) He contends that 22 “[d]ue process requires Respondents to afford Petitioner a hearing before a neutral 23 decisionmaker where ICE is required to justify re-detention before it occurs.” (Id.) 24 In evaluating similar due process claims, courts employ the three-part test set 25 forth in Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976). See, e.g., Yagman v. Garcetti, 26 852 F.3d 859, 864 (9th Cir. 2017). Under Mathews, courts evaluate (1) the private 27 interest affected by the official action; (2) the risk of an erroneous deprivation; and 28 5 Case 2:26-cv-00757-ODW-AGR Document 6 #:95 Filed 01/27/26 Page 6 of 9 Page ID 1 (3) the Government’s interest and the fiscal and administrative burdens that the 2 additional or substitute procedural requirement entail. Mathews, 424 U.S. at 335. 3 4 5 a) Private Interest Petitioner argues that he “has an exceptionally strong interest in freedom from physical confinement.” (TRO 8.) The Court agrees. 6 The Fifth Amendment protects all persons from being “deprived of life, liberty, 7 or property, without due process of law.” U.S. Const. amend. V. It is settled law that 8 noncitizens within the United States are entitled to due process “whether their 9 presence here is lawful, unlawful, temporary, or permanent.” Zadvydas v. Davis, 10 533 U.S. 678, 693 (2001); see Reno v. Flores, 507 U.S. 292, 306 (1993) (“It is well 11 established that the Fifth Amendment entitles aliens to due process of law in the 12 context of [removal] proceedings.”). The government’s release of an individual from 13 detention creates “an implicit promise’ that the individual’s liberty will be revoked 14 only if they fail to abide by the conditions of their release.” Calderon v. Kaiser, 15 No. 25-cv-06695-AMO, 2025 WL 2430609, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 22, 2025) (quoting 16 Morrissey v. Brewer, 408 U.S. 471, 482 (1972)). 17 When Petitioner was released on parole from his initial detention, he acquired a 18 liberty interest which entitles him to due process. Doe v. Becerra, 787 F. Supp. 3d 19 1083, 1093 (E.D. Cal. 2025) (“The Supreme Court has repeatedly recognized that 20 individuals who have been released from custody, even where such release is 21 conditional, have a liberty interest in their continued liberty.”). As Petitioner has an 22 interest in continued liberty, the procedures used against him must adequately protect 23 that interest. See Shaughnessy v. United States ex rel. Mezei, 345 U.S. 206, 212 24 (1953) (noting that a noncitizen “may be expelled only after proceedings conforming 25 to traditional standards of fairness encompassed in due process of law”). 26 Respondents re-detained Petitioner without notice or a pre-deprivation hearing. 27 (TRO 2); see Pinchi v. Noem, 792 F. Supp. 3d 1025, 1033 (N.D. Cal. 2025) (holding 28 that a noncitizen has a “constitutional right to a hearing before a neutral 6 Here, Case 2:26-cv-00757-ODW-AGR Document 6 #:96 Filed 01/27/26 Page 7 of 9 Page ID 1 decisionmaker prior to any future detention”). Thus, Petitioner has a strong interest in 2 his liberty, and any deprivation of that interest must comport with due process. 3 4 5 b) Risk of Erroneous Deprivation Petitioner argues that his re-detention without a pre-deprivation hearing results in a high risk of erroneous deprivation. (TRO 10–11.) The Court agrees. 6 Where an individual “has not received any bond or custody redetermination 7 hearing, the risk of an erroneous deprivation of liberty is high.” Pablo Sequen v. 8 Albarran, No. 25-cv-06487-PCP, 2025 WL 2935630, at *11 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 15, 2025) 9 (citation modified). Civil immigration detention, which is “nonpunitive in purpose 10 and effect,” is justified only when a noncitizen presents a risk of flight or danger to the 11 community. See Zadvydas, 533 U.S. at 690. 12 Here, Petitioner was released on parole after Respondents determined that he 13 was not a flight risk or danger to the community. (Pet. ¶ 1.) Before his re-detention, 14 Petitioner did not receive notice of Respondents’ intention to re-detain him and had no 15 opportunity to contest Respondents’ action. (See id. ¶ 5; TRO 2.) 16 Moreover, ICE arrested Petitioner during a scheduled check-in. (Pet. ¶ 33.) 17 Respondents’ belief that they had a valid reason to detain him does not eliminate their 18 obligation to effectuate the detention in a manner that comports with due process. See 19 M.R. v. Kaiser, 791 F. Supp. 3d 1021, 1036 (N.D. Cal. 2025) (“[A]bsent evidence of 20 urgent concerns, a pre-deprivation hearing is required to satisfy due process.”). As 21 Petitioner has not been provided notice and a pre-deprivation hearing to determine 22 whether his re-detention is warranted based on flight risk or danger to community, the 23 Court finds that the risk of erroneous deprivation is high. 24 c) Respondents’ Interest 25 Finally, Respondents’ interest in re-detaining Petitioner’s without first providing 26 him with notice and a custody hearing is minimal. Respondents could not identify any 27 “legitimate interest that would support detaining [Petitioner] without a pre-detention 28 7 Case 2:26-cv-00757-ODW-AGR Document 6 #:97 Filed 01/27/26 Page 8 of 9 Page ID 1 hearing.” See Calderon, 2025 WL 2430609, at *4. Nor can Respondents claim that 2 providing a pre-detention hearing would be an administrative or financial burden. Id. 3 In sum, the Court finds that Petitioner has shown that, under Mathews, he was 4 entitled to notice and an opportunity to be heard before Respondents re-detained him. 5 As Respondents failed to provide Petitioner with notice and a pre-deprivation hearing, 6 Petitioner has shown a likelihood of success on the merits of his due process claim. 7 2. 8 As to the second Winter factor, Petitioner contends that he will suffer 9 irreparable harm in the absence of a TRO because he will continue to be unlawfully 10 Likelihood of Irreparable Harm detained and separated from his family and friends. (TRO 13–14.) 11 “It is well established that the deprivation of constitutional rights 12 ‘unquestionably constitutes irreparable injury.’” Melendres v. Arpaio, 695 F.3d 990, 13 1002 (9th Cir. 2012) (quoting Elrod v. Burns, 427 U.S. 347, 373 (1976)). “[I]n cases 14 involving a constitutional claim, a likelihood of success on the merits usually 15 establishes irreparable harm.” Baird, 81 F.4th at 1048. 16 As discussed above, Petitioner brings a due process claim which is likely to 17 succeed on the merits. Thus, the Court finds that he has established irreparable harm, 18 and the second Winter factor also weighs in favor of temporary injunctive relief. 19 3. 20 The last two Winter factors “merge when the Government is the opposing 21 party.” Nken v. Holder, 556 U.S. 418, 435 (2009). Public interest concerns exist 22 “when a constitutional right has been violated, because all citizens have a stake in 23 upholding the Constitution.” 24 2005)). “[T]he public has a strong interest in upholding procedural protections against 25 unlawful detention,” and “in the efficient allocation” of resources. Vargas v. Jennings, 26 No. 20-cv-5785-PJH, 2020 WL 5074312, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 23, 2020). 27 28 Balance of Equities and Public Interest Preminger v. Principi, 422 F.3d 815, 826 (9th Cir. The balance of hardships tips strongly in Petitioner’s favor as he would suffer great hardship if the Court were to deny his TRO. 8 See Winter, 555 U.S. at 26 Case 2:26-cv-00757-ODW-AGR Document 6 #:98 Filed 01/27/26 Page 9 of 9 Page ID 1 (requiring the balance of hardships to “tip strongly” in the moving party’s favor). 2 Specifically, Petitioner would continue to be detained for an indefinite amount of time 3 without due process. (TRO 14.) Should Petitioner remain detained without due 4 process, “neither equity nor the public’s interest are furthered by allowing violations 5 of federal law to continue.” Galvez v. Jaddou, 52 F.4th 821, 832 (9th Cir. 2022). 6 Thus, the balance of equities and the public interest factors also favor injunctive relief. 7 Having found that all Winter factors weigh in favor of injunctive relief, the 8 Court GRANTS Petitioner’s TRO. 9 V. 10 11 CONCLUSION For the reasons discussed above, the Court GRANTS Petitioner’s TRO. (Dkt. No. 2.) It is hereby ORDERED that: 12 Respondents shall IMMEDIATELY RELEASE Petitioner; 13 Respondents are ENJOINED from re-detaining Petitioner absent 14 compliance with constitutional protections, which include, a

Wright, II: Court DENIES Ashford's Motion and ORDERS Ashford's counsel to SHOW CAUSE why the Court should not sanction him under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b)(2). As the Guerrero court clearly states that it does not agree with the Mattson court's analysis, Ashford's counsel's attempt to pass off a passage from Mattson as Guerrero's holding is arguably frivolous. title: Richard Bonomini v. General Motors LLC et al, No. 2:2025cv09047 - Document 27 (C.D. Cal. 2026)
body: Log In Sign Up Find a Lawyer Ask a Lawyer Research the Law Law Schools Laws & Regs Newsletters Marketing Solutions Justia Connect Pro Membership Practice Membership Public Membership Justia Lawyer Directory Platinum Placements Gold Placements Justia Elevate SEO Websites Blogs Justia Amplify PPC Management Google Business Profile Social Media Justia Onward Blog Justia › U.S. Law › Case Law › Federal Courts › District Courts › California › Central District of California › 2026 › Richard Bonomini v. General Motors LLC et al › Filing 27 Richard Bonomini v. General Motors LLC et al, No. 2:2025cv09047 - Document 27 (C.D. Cal. 2026) Full Name: Richard Bonomini v. General Motors LLC et al Docket Number: 2:2025cv09047 Date: January 26, 2026 Court Description: MINUTES IN CHAMBERS) ORDER DENYING Motion to Remand (Doc. 15 ) by Judge Josephine L. Staton: Defendant shows by a preponderance of the evidence that there is diversity of citizenship and that the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000. The Court therefore has subject matter jurisdiction. Plaintiff's Motion is DENIED. (jp) Download PDF Richard Bonomini v. General Motors LLC et al Doc. 27 UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT CENTRAL DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA CIVIL MINUTES – GENERAL Case No. 2:25-cv-09047-JLS-SK Title: Richard Bonomini v. General Motors LLC et al Date: January 26, 2026 Present: Honorable JOSEPHINE L. STATON, UNITED STATES DISTRICT JUDGE Kelly Davis Deputy Clerk ATTORNEYS PRESENT FOR PLAINTIFF: Not Present N/A Court Reporter ATTORNEYS PRESENT FOR DEFENDANT: Not Present PROCEEDINGS: (IN CHAMBERS) ORDER DENYING MOTION TO REMAND (Doc. 15) Before the Court is a Motion to Remand filed by Plaintiff Richard Bonomini. (Mot., Doc. 15.) Defendant General Motors LLC opposed, and Plaintiff replied. (Opp., Doc. 18; Reply, Doc. 23.) Having taken the matter under submission, and for the following reasons, the Court DENIES Plaintiff’s Motion. I. BACKGROUND On May 9, 2025, Plaintiff Richard Bonomini filed this action in Los Angeles County Superior Court against Defendant General Motors LLC, alleging violations of the Song-Beverly Act, Cal. Civ. Code § 1793.2, and a breach of the implied warranty of merchantability, arising out of Plaintiff’s purchase of a 2022 Chevrolet Trailblazer (the “Subject Vehicle”). (See Compl., Doc. 1-1.) Plaintiff alleges that he is a “resident of La Mesa, California.” (Id. ¶ 2.) The Complaint contains no allegations as to the amount in controversy, but includes a demand for “Plaintiff’s actual damages,” “a civil penalty in the amount of two times Plaintiff’s actual damages,” and attorneys’ fees. (Id. at 7.) Defendant removed the action to federal court on September 23, 2025, invoking the Court’s diversity jurisdiction pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1332. (NOR, Doc. 1.) The ______________________________________________________________________________ CIVIL MINUTES – GENERAL 1 Dockets.Justia.com UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT CENTRAL DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA CIVIL MINUTES – GENERAL Case No. 2:25-cv-09047-JLS-SK Title: Richard Bonomini v. General Motors LLC et al Date: January 26, 2026 Notice of Removal states that complete diversity of citizenship exists because Plaintiff is a citizen of California and Defendant is a citizen of Michigan and Delaware. (Id. at 3.) It further states that the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000, based on an estimated $27,616.61 in actual damages, civil penalties in the amount of two times Plaintiff’s actual damages, and attorneys’ fees. (Id. at 5–6.) Plaintiff moved to remand the case on October 17, 2025, arguing that removal was untimely and that Defendant failed to show that the requisite threshold for the amount in controversy was met. 1 (See Mot.) On January 12, 2026, the Court directed the parties to review its previous orders, and to meet and confer to identify the remaining contested issues in this action. (Order Requiring Supp. Briefing at 1, Doc. 25.) The parties filed a joint supplemental brief on January 23, 2026, in which Plaintiff conceded that Defendant’s removal was timely, but nevertheless contested Defendant’s showing as to the amount in controversy. (Supp. Brief at 2–3, Doc. 26.) II. LEGAL STANDARD A defendant may remove a case that was filed in state court to a federal court in the same district and division if the federal court would have had original jurisdiction over the action. See 28 U.S.C. § 1441(a)–(b); Caterpillar Inc. v. Williams, 482 U.S. 386, 392 (1987). Generally, subject matter jurisdiction is based on the presence of a federal question, see 28 U.S.C. § 1331, or complete diversity between the parties, see 28 U.S.C. § 1332. A federal court has diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332 if the parties to the action are citizens of different states and the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000. See 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a). 1 Plaintiff repeatedly references the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act (“MMWA”) in his motion to remand, stating that “Plaintiff’s initial Complaint contained a Federal cause of action under the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act,” despite having brought no MMWA claim in this action. (Mot. at 2, 6, 7, 13–14.) ______________________________________________________________________________ CIVIL MINUTES – GENERAL 2 UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT CENTRAL DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA CIVIL MINUTES – GENERAL Case No. 2:25-cv-09047-JLS-SK Title: Richard Bonomini v. General Motors LLC et al Date: January 26, 2026 A removing defendant’s Notice of Removal must include “plausible allegations of the jurisdictional elements.” Acad. of Country Music v. Cont’l Cas. Co., 991 F.3d 1059, 1069 (9th Cir. 2021). “[T]he amount in controversy allegation of a defendant seeking federal-court adjudication should be accepted when not contested by the plaintiff or questioned by the court.” Dart Cherokee Basin Operating Co., LLC v. Owens, 574 U.S. 81, 82 (2014); see also id. (applying Dart Cherokee outside the CAFA context). “In the event that the plaintiff does contest the defendant’s allegations, both sides submit proof and the court decides, by a preponderance of the evidence, whether the amount-incontroversy requirement has been satisfied.” Dart Cherokee, 574 U.S. at 82. III. ANALYSIS Plaintiff challenges only whether this Court possesses diversity jurisdiction over this action. (See Supp. Brief at 2–3.) As noted above, to fall within this Court’s diversity jurisdiction, an action must be between citizens of different states and have an amount in controversy that exceeds $75,000. 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a). “The natural person’s state citizenship is [ ] determined by her state of domicile . . . [a] person’s domicile is her permanent home, where she resides with the intention to remain or to which she intends to return.” Kanter v. Warner-Lambert Co., 265 F.3d 853, 857 (9th Cir. 2001). Plaintiff’s Complaint states that he resides in La Mesa, California, and Defendant’s Notice of Removal states that “Plaintiff resided in California when he purchased the subject vehicle, and on other occasions, establishing a plausible basis for intent to remain in California[.]” (Compl. ¶ 2; NOR at 3.) With its opposition to Plaintiff’s motion to remand, Defendant also provides a copy of Plaintiff’s Retail Installment Sale Contract (“RISC”), indicating that Plaintiff bought the Subject Vehicle in Irvine, California. (Ex. A to Salas Decl., RISC, Doc. 18-2.) Plaintiff does not contest Defendant’s conclusion as to his citizenship in any of his briefs, nor does he ______________________________________________________________________________ CIVIL MINUTES – GENERAL 3 UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT CENTRAL DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA CIVIL MINUTES – GENERAL Case No. 2:25-cv-09047-JLS-SK Title: Richard Bonomini v. General Motors LLC et al Date: January 26, 2026 provide any additional evidence. Defendant’s unrebutted assertions support a finding of Plaintiff’s California citizenship. See Lopez v. Ford Motor Co., 2025 WL 3022849, at *3 (C.D. Cal. Oct. 28, 2025) (Staton, J.). “[A]n LLC is a citizen of every state of which its owners/members are citizens.” Johnson v. Columbia Props. Anchorage, LP, 437 F.3d 894, 899 (9th Cir. 2006). Defendant’s Notice of Removal provides that it is a limited liability company whose “sole member is General Motors Holdings LLC.” (NOR at 3.) “General Motors Holdings LLC’s sole member is General Motors Company. General Motors Company is a Delaware Corporation with its principal place of business in Michigan,” meaning that it is a citizen of Michigan and Delaware. (Id.); see 28 U.S.C. § 1332(c)(1). The Court is therefore satisfied that Defendant has sufficiently alleged complete diversity of citizenship between Defendant, which, like its members, is a citizen of Michigan and Delaware, and Plaintiff, who is a citizen of California. Turning to the amount in controversy, “[t]he measure of a buyer’s damages in [a Song-Beverly Act] action includes ‘replacement or reimbursement as set forth in subdivision (d) of Section 1793.2[.]’” Niedermeier v. FCA US LLC, 15 Cal. 5th 792, 800 (2024). Under that subdivision, reimbursement or restitution is “an amount equal to the actual price paid or payable by the buyer[.]” Cal. Civ. Code § 1793.2(d)(2)(B); Cal. Civ. Code § 1794(b). The “amount directly attributable to use by the buyer prior to the discovery of the nonconformity” must be subtracted from the calculation of actual damages. Id. § 1793.2(d)(1). As of January 1, 2025, in addition to mileage use offsets, “additional offsets exist for negative equity; manufacturers’ rebates and credits; and the actual price of ‘optional equipment, service contracts, or [guaranteed asset protection] financing purchased by the plaintiff.’” Diaz v. Nissan N. Am., Inc., 2025 WL 2647458, at *3 (C.D. Cal. Sept. 12, 2025) (quoting Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 871.27(b)–(d)). Manufacturers can, and Defendant here has, “elect[ed] to be governed” by these additional offsets for all cars “sold in the year 2025 and in all prior years[.]” Cal. Civ. ______________________________________________________________________________ CIVIL MINUTES – GENERAL 4 UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT CENTRAL DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA CIVIL MINUTES – GENERAL Case No. 2:25-cv-09047-JLS-SK Title: Richard Bonomini v. General Motors LLC et al Date: January 26, 2026 Proc. Code § 871.30(a); (see Opp. at 24). The Song-Beverly Act also provides for civil penalties of up to double the amount of actual damages, as well as for attorneys’ fees. See Cal. Civ. Code § 1794(c)–(d). The evidence provided by Defendant shows that the amount of actual damages in controversy is $26,128.71. 2 Defendant asserts that, after including civil penalties of up to two times actual damages, as well as attorneys’ fees, the amount in controversy exceeds the $75,000 threshold. (NOR at 4–6; Opp. at 26–28.) “The civil penalty under California Civil Code § 1794(c) cannot simply be assumed.” Pennon v. Subaru of Am., Inc., 2022 WL 2208578, at *2 (C.D. Cal. June 17, 2022). Rather, “[t]o satisfy its burden, the removing party must make some effort to justify the assumption by, for example, pointing to allegations in the complaint suggesting award of a civil penalty would be appropriate, and providing evidence—such as verdicts or judgments from similar cases—regarding the likely amount of the penalty.” Id. (internal citation and quotation omitted). To satisfy this burden, Defendant points to Plaintiff’s allegations of willfulness, the fact that “the Subject Vehicle was presented for repair at least 8 times[,]” and its 2 In its opposition, Defendant calculates $31,126.31 of actual damages at issue, by subtracting mileage offsets and offsets for third-party service contracts from the Subject Vehicle’s purchase price of $39,750.60. (Opp. at 26–27.) However, the damages calculation should use the total cash price in the RISC, see Galaviz v. Gen. Motors, LLC, 2025 WL 3022665, at *3 (C.D. Cal. Oct. 28, 2025) (Staton, J.), which is $36,944.20. (RISC at 2.) Moreover, Defendant is not entitled only to mileage and third-party service contract offsets, but also to offsets for third-party theft-deterrent devices and surface-protection products. Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 871.27(b)(1). Thus, by subtracting an offset of $6,187 for third-party service contracts, an offset of $995 for third-party surface-protection products, an offset of $1,295 for third-party SWAT theft-deterrent protection, and a mileage offset of $2,338.29, from the Subject Vehicle’s Total Cash Price of $36,944.20, the Court calculates that there are $26,128.71 of actual damages at issue. (RISC at 2; Opp. at 27.) ______________________________________________________________________________ CIVIL MINUTES – GENERAL 5 UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT CENTRAL DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA CIVIL MINUTES – GENERAL Case No. 2:25-cv-09047-JLS-SK Title: Richard Bonomini v. General Motors LLC et al Date: January 26, 2026 counsel’s experience that “plaintiffs pursue civil penalties where there are records of multiple repair presentations.” (See Compl. ¶¶ 17, 24, 28; Salas Decl. ¶¶ 3, 6, Doc. 18-1; Ex. B to Salas Decl., Doc. 18-3.) As the Court has concluded in other cases, such allegations adequately support the inclusion of civil penalties in the amount in controversy. See, e.g., Lopez, 2025 WL 3022849, at *4. The Court therefore calculates a potential amount in controversy of at least $78,386.12. Defendant shows by a preponderance of the evidence that there is diversity of citizenship and that the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000. The Court therefore has subject matter jurisdiction. IV. CONCLUSION For the above reasons, Plaintiff’s Motion is DENIED. Correctional Officer Drayton et al Doc. 64 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT 9 CENTRAL DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA 10 11 12 Plaintiff, 13 14 15 Case No. 2:21-cv-06020-ODW-JC JEREMY JONES, v. MEMORANDUM OPINION AND ORDER DISMISSING ACTION CORRECTIONAL OFFICER DRAYTON, et al., 16 Defendants. 17 18 I. 19 BACKGROUND AND SUMMARY On July 23, 2021, Plaintiff Jeremy Jones, a California inmate who is 20 proceeding pro se and has been granted leave to proceed without prepayment of the 21 filing fee, filed a Civil Rights Complaint (“Complaint” or “Comp.”) pursuant to 22 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1983 and 1985 against nine California Department of 23 Corrections and Rehabilitation employees working at the California State Prison, 24 Los Angeles County in Lancaster, California (“CSP-LAC”): Correctional Officers 25 Drayton, Penate, Bowden, and Santamaria; Correctional Sergeants Aguirre and 26 Almos; Correctional Lieutenants Mijuarez and Martinez; and Assistant Warden 27 Jordan. (Docket (“Dkt.”) No. 1; Comp. at 1-4 (as paginated on the Court’s 28 electronic docket)). Dockets.Justia.com 1 On February 15, 2022, the assigned United States Magistrate Judge 2 (“Magistrate Judge”) – pursuant to 28 U.S.C. §§ 1915(e)(2) and 1915A – screened 3 and dismissed the Complaint with leave to amend since, among other things, the 4 Complaint violated Rule 8 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. (Dkt. No. 8).1 5 On June 7, 2022, Plaintiff filed a First Amended Complaint (alternatively, 6 “FAC”) pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (“Section 1983”) against the Defendants 7 named in the original Complaint – Jordan, Martinez, Mijuarez, Aguirre, Almos, 8 Drayton, Penate, Bowden, and Santamaria – and seven new CSP-LAC employees: 9 Correctional Officers Rosas, Mimaki, Kouzmitch, Serrano, Carreon, Root, and 10 Galvan. (Dkt. No. 16; FAC at 3-8 (as paginated on the Court’s electronic docket)). 11 On February 27, 2023, the Magistrate Judge screened the First Amended 12 Complaint and dismissed it with leave to amend due to multiple deficiencies, 13 including violations of Rules 8 and 10 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. 14 (Dkt. No. 17).2 15 On August 7, 2023, Plaintiff filed a Second Amended Complaint 16 (alternatively, “SAC”), again suing the same sixteen Defendants named in the First 17 Amended Complaint in their individual and official capacities. (Dkt. No. 26). 18 On June 28, 2024, all Defendants other than unserved Defendant Drayton 19 (“Defendants”), filed a Motion to Dismiss the Second Amended Complaint 20 (“Motion to Dismiss”). (Dkt. No. 43). On July 19, 2024, Plaintiff filed an 21 Opposition to the Motion to Dismiss. (Dkt. No. 46). On August 2, 2024, 22 Defendants filed a Reply. (Dkt. No. 47). 23 On June 4, 2025, the Magistrate Judge issued a Report and Recommendation, 24 recommending that the Court grant in part and deny in part the Motion to Dismiss. 25 (Dkt. No. 52). On June 5, 2025, the Magistrate Judge also issued an Order to Show 26 27 1 28 2 This Court agrees with and adopts the Magistrate Judge’s February 15, 2022 Order. This Court agrees with and adopts the Magistrate Judge’s February 27, 2023 Order. 2 1 Cause directing Plaintiff to show cause why this action should not be dismissed as 2 against unserved Defendant Drayton. (Dkt. No. 53). The Magistrate Judge 3 extended Plaintiff’s deadlines to file objections to the Report and Recommendation 4 and a response to the Order to Show Cause multiple times. (Dkt. Nos. 55, 60). 5 Ultimately, Plaintiff neither filed objections to the Report and Recommendation nor 6 a response to the Order to Show Cause. 7 On October 27, 2025, this Court issued an Order (“October Order”) 8 (1) dismissing this action without prejudice as against Defendant Drayton based on 9 Plaintiff’s failure to respond to the Order to Show Cause and to provide accurate 10 and sufficient information to enable service of the operative complaint and 11 summons to be effected on Defendant Drayton, Plaintiff’s failure to prosecute this 12 action as against Defendant Drayton, and Plaintiff’s failure timely to comply with 13 the Magistrate Judge’s June 10, 2024 Order directing Plaintiff to supply the Court 14 with information sufficient to effect service upon such Defendant; (2) accepting the 15 Report and Recommendation and granting in part and denying in part Defendants’ 16 Motion to Dismiss; (3) directing Plaintiff, within twenty (20) days (i.e., by 17 November 17, 2025) to file a Third Amended Complaint or a Notice of Intent to 18 Proceed Solely on Remaining Claims; and (4) cautioning Plaintiff, in bold-face 19 print, that Plaintiff’s failure timely to file a Third Amended Complaint or a Notice 20 of Intent to Proceed Solely on Remaining Claims may result in the dismissal of this 21 action in whole or in part, with or without prejudice, on the grounds set forth in the 22 Report and Recommendation, on the ground that amendment is futile, for failure 23 diligently to prosecute and/or for failure to comply with the October Order. (Dkt. 24 61). 25 On November 17, 2025, Plaintiff filed an unverified notice and request for 26 extension claiming that he had filed a Third Amended Complaint and response to 27 the Order to Show Cause on September 26, 2025 – items the Court has never 28 received – and requesting an extension of time to resubmit such items and to move 3 1 for reconsideration. (Dkt. No. 62). The Magistrate Judge granted Plaintiff’s 2 request, extended Plaintiff’s deadline to comply with the October Order to 3 December 24, 2025, set December 24, 2025 as the deadline for Plaintiff to seek 4 reconsideration, and again cautioned Plaintiff in bold-face print that his failure 5 timely to file a Third Amended Complaint or a Notice of Intent to Proceed Solely 6 on Remaining Claims may result in the dismissal of this action in whole or in part, 7 with or without prejudice, on the grounds set forth in the Report and 8 Recommendation, on the ground that amendment is futile, for failure diligently to 9 prosecute and/or for failure to comply with the October Order. (Dkt. No. 63). 10 Although the extended deadline to comply with the October Order and the 11 deadline to file a motion for reconsideration expired weeks ago, to date, the Court 12 has not received a Third Amended Complaint, a Notice of Intent to Proceed Solely 13 on Remaining Claims, a response to the Order to Show Cause, or a motion for 14 reconsideration from Plaintiff. Nor has it received any other requests from Plaintiff 15 since his November 17, 2025 submission. 16 As discussed below, this action is dismissed due to Plaintiff’s unreasonable 17 failure to prosecute and his failure to comply with the October Order by the 18 extended deadline to do so. 19 II. PERTINENT LAW 20 It is well-established that a district court may sua sponte dismiss an action 21 where the plaintiff has failed to comply with a court order and/or unreasonably 22 failed to prosecute. See Link v. Wabash Railroad Co., 370 U.S. 626, 629-33 23 (1962); Ferdik v. Bonzelet, 963 F.2d 1258, 1260 (9th Cir.) (as amended), cert. 24 denied, 506 U.S. 915 (1992); see also McKeever v. Block, 932 F.2d 795, 797 (9th 25 Cir. 1991) (district court may sua sponte dismiss action “only for an unreasonable 26 failure to prosecute”) (citations omitted); see also Edwards v. Marin Park, Inc., 356 27 F.3d 1058, 1065 (9th Cir. 2004) (sua sponte dismissal pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 28 41(b) proper sanction in cases where a plaintiff is notified of deficiencies in 4 1 complaint and is given “the opportunity to amend [the complaint] or be dismissed” 2 but the plaintiff “[does] nothing”) (citations omitted; emphasis in original). 3 In determining whether to dismiss an action for failure to prosecute or failure 4 to comply with court orders, a district court must consider several factors, namely 5 (1) the public’s interest in expeditious resolution of litigation; (2) the court’s need 6 to manage its docket; (3) the risk of prejudice to defendants; (4) the public policy 7 favoring disposition of cases on their merits; and (5) the availability of less drastic 8 alternatives. See In re Eisen, 31 F.3d 1447, 1451 (9th Cir. 1994) (failure to 9 prosecute); Ferdik, 963 F.2d at 1260-61 (failure to comply with court orders). 10 Dismissal is appropriate under the foregoing analysis “where at least four factors 11 support dismissal . . . or where at least three factors ‘strongly’ support dismissal.” 12 Hernandez v. City of El Monte, 138 F.3d 393, 399 (9th Cir. 1998) (citations 13 omitted). 14 Where a plaintiff is proceeding pro se, however, the court must first notify 15 the plaintiff of the deficiencies in the complaint so that the plaintiff has an 16 opportunity “to amend effectively.” Ferdik, 963 F.2d at 1261 (citation omitted). A 17 District Judge may not dismiss an action for failure to comply with a court order or 18 for unreasonable failure to prosecute if the initial decision to dismiss a complaint 19 was erroneous. Yourish v. California Amplifier, 191 F.3d 983, 992 (9th Cir. 1999) 20 (citing id.). 21 III. DISCUSSION AND ORDER 22 First, the Court has reviewed its October Order, and finds that it adequately 23 and properly notified Plaintiff of the deficiencies in the Second Amended 24 Complaint, dismissed the deficient portions thereof, and afforded Plaintiff leave to 25 amend or to notify the Court that he wished to proceed solely on the remaining 26 claims therein. 27 Second, dismissal is appropriate based upon Plaintiff’s failure to comply with 28 the October Order and the failure to prosecute. The Court has considered the five 5 1 factors discussed above – the public’s interest in expeditious resolution of litigation, 2 the court’s need to manage its docket, the risk of prejudice to the Defendants, the 3 public policy favoring disposition of cases on their merits, and the availability of 4 less drastic alternatives. The first two factors – the public’s interest in expeditiously 5 resolving this litigation and the Court’s interest in managing the docket – strongly 6 weigh in favor of dismissal. As noted above, Plaintiff has been notified of the 7 deficiencies in the Second Amended Complaint and has been given the opportunity 8 to amend it or to notify the Court that he wishes to stand solely on the remaining 9 claims therein. There is no evidence in the record to establish that he has done 10 either. See Edwards, 356 F.3d at 1065. The third factor, risk of prejudice to the 11 Defendants, also weighs strongly in favor of dismissal. See Anderson v. Air West, 12 Inc., 542 F.2d 522, 524 (9th Cir. 1976) (prejudice to defendants presumed from 13 unreasonable delay) (citation omitted). The fourth factor, the public policy favoring 14 disposition of cases on their merits, is greatly outweighed by the factors in favor of 15 dismissal discussed herein. As for the fifth factor, since Plaintiff has already been 16 cautioned of the consequences of his failure to prosecute and his failure to comply 17 with the October Order by the deadline/extended deadline to do so, and has been 18 afforded the opportunity to avoid such consequences but has not responded, no 19 sanction lesser than dismissal is feasible. See, e.g., Yourish, 191 F.3d at 989 20 (dismissal of action with prejudice not excessive sanction for plaintiffs’ failure 21 timely to comply with court’s order to submit an amended complaint). 22 IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED that this action is dismissed based upon 23 Plaintiff’s unreasonable failure to prosecute and his failure to comply with the 24 October Order by the extended deadline to do so. 25 IT IS SO ORDERED. 26 DATED: _January 26, 2026 27 ________________________________________ 28 HONORABLE OTIS D. title: Sara Amar Fahmy v. Frank Bisignano, No. 2:2025cv06001 - Document 18 (C.D. Cal. 2026)
body: Log In Sign Up Find a Lawyer Ask a Lawyer Research the Law Law Schools Laws & Regs Newsletters Marketing Solutions Justia Connect Pro Membership Practice Membership Public Membership Justia Lawyer Directory Platinum Placements Gold Placements Justia Elevate SEO Websites Blogs Justia Amplify PPC Management Google Business Profile Social Media Justia Onward Blog Justia › U.S. Law › Case Law › Federal Courts › District Courts › California › Central District of California › 2026 › Sara Amar Fahmy v. Frank Bisignano › Filing 18 Sara Amar Fahmy v. Frank Bisignano, No. 2:2025cv06001 - Document 18 (C.D. Cal. 2026) Full Name: Sara Amar Fahmy v. Frank Bisignano Docket Number: 2:2025cv06001 Date: January 21, 2026 Court Description: MEMORANDUM OPINION AND ORDER by Magistrate Judge Douglas F. McCormick, The agency's denial of benefits is affirmed and this action is dismissed with prejudice. (SEE DOCUMENT FOR DETAILS) (sh) Download PDF Sara Amar Fahmy v. Frank Bisignano Doc. 18 UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT CENTRAL DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA WESTERN DIVISION SARA F., Case No. CV 25-06001-DFM Plaintiff, MEMORANDUM OPINION AND ORDER v. FRANK BISIGNANO, Commissioner of Social Security, Defendant. Plaintiff Sara F. appeals the Commissioner’s decision denying her application for supplemental security income.1 For the reasons set forth below, the Court affirms the agency’s denial of benefits and dismisses this action with prejudice. BACKGROUND Plaintiff applied for supplemental security income on November 7, 2022, alleging disability beginning September 3, 2018. See Dkt. 11, Administrative Record (“AR”) 195-204.2 The Commissioner denied the claim initially on The Court partially redacts Plaintiff’s name in compliance with Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 5.2(c)(2)(B) and the recommendation of the Committee on Court Administration and Case Management of the Judicial Conference of the United States. 1 2 Citations to the AR are to the record pagination. All other docket Dockets.Justia.com March 2, 2023, see AR 94-99, and upon reconsideration on January 19, 2024, see AR 101-08. Thereafter, Plaintiff requested and received a hearing before an administrative law judge (“ALJ”) on August 8, 2024. See AR 44-64. The ALJ issued an unfavorable decision on December 30, 2024. See AR 28-43. The ALJ followed the five-step sequential evaluation process for determining whether an individual is disabled. See 20 C.F.R. § 416.920(a). At step one, the ALJ found that Plaintiff had not engaged in substantial gainful activity since November 7, 2022, the application date. See AR 33. At step two, the ALJ found that Plaintiff had the severe impairments of “degenerative disc disease and right shoulder strain.” AR 34. At step three, the ALJ found that Plaintiff did not have an impairment or combination of impairments that met or medically equaled the severity of one of the listed impairments in 20 C.F.R. Part 404, Subpart P, Appendix 1. See id. After considering the record, the ALJ found that Plaintiff had the residual functional capacity (“RFC”) to perform light work as defined in 20 C.F.R. § 416.967(b) except “she can only occasionally reach over head; she can only occasionally perform postural activities.” Id. At step four, the ALJ found that Plaintiff had no past relevant work. See AR 37. At step five, considering Plaintiff’s documented vocational background and the opinion of a vocational expert, the ALJ found that there are jobs that exist in significant numbers in the national economy that Plaintiff could perform, including cashier II; sales attendant; and cleaner, housekeeping. See AR 37-38. Consequently, the ALJ found that Plaintiff had not been under a disability since November 7, 2022, the application date. See AR 38. The Appeals Council denied review of the ALJ’s decision. See AR 1-6. Plaintiff then sought judicial review from this Court. See Dkt. 1. citations are to the CM/ECF pagination. 2 LEGAL STANDARD A district court will set aside a denial of benefits only if “it is either not supported by substantial evidence or is based upon legal error.” Luther v. Berryhill, 891 F.3d 872, 875 (9th Cir. 2018) (citation omitted). Under the substantial-evidence standard, the district court looks to the existing administrative record and determines “whether it contains sufficient evidence to support the agency’s factual determinations.” Biestek v. Berryhill, 587 U.S. 97, 102 (2019) (citation omitted) (cleaned up). “Substantial” means “more than a mere scintilla” but only “such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion.” Id. at 103 (citation omitted). This threshold “is not high” and “defers to the presiding ALJ, who has seen the hearing up close.” Id. at 103, 108. “Where evidence is susceptible to more than one rational interpretation, it is the ALJ’s conclusion that must be upheld.” Burch v. Barnhart, 400 F.3d 676, 679 (9th Cir. 2005) (citation omitted). DISCUSSION The parties’ sole dispute is whether the ALJ properly considered Plaintiff’s subjective symptom testimony. See Dkt. 13, Plaintiff’s Brief (“Pl.’s Br.”); Dkt. 17, Defendant’s Brief (“Def.’s Br.”). Applicable Law The ALJ applies a two-step analysis to assess a claimant’s credibility for symptom severity. See Trevizo v. Berryhill, 871 F.3d 664, 678 (9th Cir. 2017). Once the claimant “has presented objective medical evidence of an underlying impairment which could reasonably be expected to produce the pain or other symptoms alleged,” then, absent evidence of malingering, “the ALJ can reject the claimant’s testimony about the severity of her symptoms only by offering specific, clear and convincing reasons for doing so.” Id. (citation omitted). “[T]he ALJ must identify what testimony is not credible and what evidence 3 undermines the claimant’s complaints.” Reddick v. Chater, 157 F.3d 715, 722 (9th Cir. 1998) (citation omitted). “The clear and convincing standard is the most demanding required in Social Security cases.” Trevizo, 871 F.3d at 678 (citation omitted). The ALJ’s findings “must be sufficiently specific to allow a reviewing court to conclude the adjudicator rejected the claimant’s testimony on permissible grounds and did not arbitrarily discredit a claimant’s testimony regarding pain.” BrownHunter v. Colvin, 806 F.3d 487, 493 (9th Cir. 2015) (citation omitted). However, “an ALJ is not required to believe every allegation of disabling pain, or else disability benefits would be available for the asking, a result plainly contrary to the Social Security Act.” Smartt v. Kijakazi, 53 F.4th 489, 499 (9th Cir. 2022) (citation and internal quotation marks omitted). The clear and convincing “standard isn’t whether our court is convinced, but instead whether the ALJ’s rationale is clear enough that it has the power to convince.” Id. Plaintiff’s Testimony The ALJ accurately summarized Plaintiff’s testimony as follows. In connection with her application for [SSI], the claimant alleged an inability to work due to back pain resulting from a car accident. She testified at a hearing held in August 2024, that she was in a car accident during which she injured her back. As a result, she has symptoms that cause her to be unable to stand long hours or lift heavy boxes. She received treatment at Venice Family Clinic and filed a lawsuit related to her car accident. She is able to stand a few hours. She feels numbness and tingling when she is sitting down. She refuses to lift heavy items and cannot pick up more than 10 pounds. She is able to do light chores around the house for a short period of time. She is able to take care of her personal hygiene. She is able to drive. She does her own grocery shopping. She testified that everything is long and tedious when her back and neck hurts. She uses heat patches. She has never received any injections or medications for pain. 4 AR 35 (internal citations omitted). Analysis The ALJ partially discredited Plaintiff’s allegations at the second Trevizo step, finding that her medically determinable impairments could reasonably be expected to cause the alleged symptoms, but that her “statements concerning the intensity, persistence and limiting effects of these symptoms are not entirely consistent with the medical evidence and other evidence in the record for the reasons explained in this decision.” AR 35. Specifically, the ALJ found that Plaintiff’s statements were inconsistent with the medical evidence and her course of treatment. See AR 35-36. First, the ALJ found that Plaintiff’s allegations “are simply not consistent with the objective clinical findings documented in the medical records.” AR 35. “When objective medical evidence in the record is inconsistent with the claimant’s subjective testimony, the ALJ may indeed weigh it as undercutting such testimony.” Smartt, 53 F.4th at 498 (emphasis omitted). The ALJ cited specific, clear, and convincing examples to establish that Plaintiff’s testimony was inconsistent with the objective medical evidence. To start, the ALJ explained that despite Plaintiff’s allegations that she has been unable to work since September 2018, she submitted no evidence of medical treatment prior to 2022. See AR 35. The ALJ further explained that the lack of evidence was “particularly notable given the claimant’s allegations of disability related to an automobile accident in 2018 during which she injured her back. There is no evidence of this event.” Id. (emphasis added). Plaintiff asserts that this is a “straw-man rationale,” as the “only relevant date for consideration of medical evidence is November 2022 and forward.” Pl.’s Br. at 9-10. Even if true, the ALJ went on to explain, “[t]here is no 5 evidence that the claimant reported symptoms related to back pain or shoulder pain to any treating medical provider at any time.” AR 35. In support, the ALJ correctly noted that the submitted medical records from Venice Urgent Care show treatment for a cold and COVID in 2022, see AR 364-86, a urinary tract infection in November 2022, see AR 319, a urinary tract infection and acute vaginitis in June 2023, see AR 334-49, and similar symptoms in August 2023, see AR 350-57, but nothing related to back or shoulder pain. See id. Like the ALJ, the Court was unable to find any mention of Plaintiff’s principal complaints and resulting limitations. What’s more, the ALJ noted that “the only medical personnel the claimant reported her allegedly disabling conditions to were those involved in the evaluation of her disability claim.” AR 35. At the request of the State agency, Plaintiff was seen for an orthopedic consultative evaluation with Jerry Chuang, M.D., in January 2023. See AR 328-33. Plaintiff complained of lower back pain radiating down both legs since a motor vehicle accident in 2018, but acknowledged she was receiving no treatment. See AR 329. Upon examination, Dr. Chuang reported that Plaintiff had a normal gait, no deficit of the cervical or thoracic spine, some tenderness and weakness of the lumbar spine, and full range of motion of both shoulders with no instability. See AR 328-33. Plaintiff was seen again for another orthopedic consultative evaluation with Dr. Chuang in January 2024, reporting similar symptoms of back pain and pain in her right shoulder. See AR 358-63. Upon examination, Plaintiff presented with similar limitations as before, including some mild weakness of the right shoulder and bilateral lower extremities. See id. Based on the above, the ALJ found that Plaintiff’s allegations of extreme functional limitations were undermined by the medical evidence, “which conspicuously fails to show a physiological basis for the extreme pain and limitation alleged.” AR 36. Plaintiff does not refute any of these findings. 6 Second, the ALJ found that Plaintiff’s “course of medical treatment in this case does not bolster the claimant’s allegations regarding the severity or persistence of her symptoms.” AR 36. An ALJ may consider “unexplained or inadequately explained failure to seek treatment or to follow a prescribed course of treatment” in weighing a claimant’s credibility. Tommasetti v. Astrue, 533 F.3d 1035, 1039 (9th Cir. 2008). The ALJ focused on the “lack of pursuit of medical treatment” for Plaintiff’s allegedly disabling conditions, noting that she had not been sent for imaging, prescribed any pain medication, attended physical therapy, or been seen by orthopedic or neurosurgical specialists. See AR 36. Additionally, the ALJ contrasted Plaintiff’s use of urgent care centers in the area with the lack of evidence suggesting she “ever complained of symptoms of back or shoulder pain to treating physicians.” Id. Plaintiff does not refute the ALJ’s assessment, which is supported by substantial evidence. Indeed, at the hearing, the ALJ repeatedly pushed Plaintiff regarding the lack of record evidence. See, e.g., AR 52 (“So in 2022, 2023, all the visits I have are for UTIs with prescriptions for that. There’s nothing about back pain.”), id. (“Did someone write you prescriptions for pain medication? Have you had x-rays?”). Ultimately, Plaintiff’s lack of treatment undermines her reports regarding the disabling nature of her pain. See Meanel v. Apfel, 172 F.3d 1111, 1114 (9th Cir. 1999) (rejecting subjective pain complaints where plaintiff’s “claim that she experienced pain approaching the highest level imaginable was inconsistent with the ‘minimal, conservative treatment’ that she received”). Plaintiff broadly argues that the ALJ merely summarized the evidence of record without addressing her specific testimony. See Pl.’s Br. at 8-10. To ensure that “appellate review is meaningful,” the ALJ is required to “specifically identify the testimony [from a claimant] she or he finds not to be credible and . . . explain what evidence undermines the testimony.” Treichler 7 v. Comm’r of Soc. Sec. Admin., 775 F.3d 1090, 1102 (9th Cir. 2014) (alterations in original) (citation omitted); see also Brown-Hunter, 806 F.3d at 493 (finding error where “the ALJ stated only that she found, based on unspecified claimant testimony and a summary of medical evidence, that ‘the functional limitations from the claimant’s impairments were less serious than she has alleged’”). This argument is not persuasive. The ALJ contrasted the specific testimony at issue—back and shoulder pain from a car accident—with the lack of record evidence to support those limitations. “Ultimately, the ‘clear and convincing’ standard requires an ALJ to show his [or her] work,” which the ALJ did here. Smartt, 53 F.4th at 499. “Not every reason need be supported by substantial evidence, but the ‘ultimate credibility determination’ must be.” Baker v. Saul, 836 F. App’x 526, 530 (9th Cir. 2020) (quoting Carmickle v. Comm’r Soc. Sec. Admin., 533 F.3d 1155, 1162 (9th Cir. 2008)). Here, the ALJ gave at least two clear and convincing reasons, supported by substantial evidence, for discounting Plaintiff’s testimony. Remand is not warranted on this claim of error. CONCLUSION The agency’s denial of benefits is affirmed and this action is dismissed with prejudice. Date: January 21, 2026 ___________________________ DOUGLAS F. McCORMICK United States Magistrate Judge 8 Some case metadata and case summaries were written with the help of AI, which can produce inaccuracies.
